claims.text: High configurational entropy stabilizes a homogeneous, simple crystalline matrix such as a bcc solid solution.
A homogeneous bcc matrix promotes robust electron-phonon-mediated Cooper pairing despite strong atomic disorder.
Lowering configurational entropy degrades the structural stabilization attributed to high entropy.
Lowering configurational entropy will lower the superconducting transition temperature.
Lowering configurational entropy will reduce the superconducting volume fraction.
The uncharacterized starting alloy is a near-equiatomic alloy of at least five transition metals with a simple disordered structure such as a bcc solid solution.
Replacing about 10 at.% of one constituent with a chemically similar element that mixes less randomly will reduce the alloy's configurational entropy.
The compositional substitution can be made while retaining the same bcc phase.
The stability of the disordered, homogeneous bcc lattice is maintained by high configurational entropy.
A high level of random atomic mixing minimizes detrimental local lattice distortions.
Random atomic mixing preserves an electronic structure that supports strong electron-phonon coupling.
Strong electron-phonon coupling enables low-temperature Cooper-pair formation in this alloy.
Reducing configurational entropy perturbs the alloy's local structure.
Entropy-induced local structural perturbations weaken electron-phonon interactions and impede superconductivity.
The lower-entropy alloy will have a lower Tc than the baseline high-entropy alloy.
The lower-entropy alloy will show a smaller superconducting volume fraction than the baseline alloy.
A diminished diamagnetic response can indicate a reduced bulk superconducting fraction.
The proposed entropy effect should hold only while the bcc solid solution is retained without secondary phases and measurements remain at approximately 2–10 K and ambient pressure.
